options.a: Transfer instruments and maintain a clear field so the operator works efficiently
options.b: Diagnose caries on radiographs and chart findings for the dentist to sign
options.c: Select the restorative material and shade based on the finished cavity preparation
options.d: Place the final restoration while the dentist prepares the next tooth

distractorExplanations.b: Assistants may chart findings the dentist calls out, but diagnosis is reserved to the dentist.
distractorExplanations.c: Material selection is a treatment decision made by the dentist; the assistant prepares and mixes the chosen material.
distractorExplanations.d: Placing restorations is an expanded function permitted by some states; it is not the core four-handed assisting role.

options.a: Retracting the gingiva to expose subgingival margins for impressions
options.b: Reducing the need for HVE suction during high-speed preparation
options.c: Improving visibility, moisture control, and airway protection
options.d: Eliminating aerosols so masks and eyewear can be reduced

distractorExplanations.a: Gingival retraction for impressions is done with retraction cord, not with a rubber dam.
distractorExplanations.b: HVE is still needed to remove spray and debris on top of the dam; the dam controls saliva, not handpiece water.
distractorExplanations.d: A dam reduces but does not eliminate aerosols; standard PPE including masks and eyewear is still required.

danb-gc-readiness-check-chairside-003.explanation: Rubber dam isolates the tooth, controls moisture, and reduces aspiration/swallowing risk. It also protects the airway from small objects.

options.a: In the vestibule of the opposite arch, away from the spray
options.b: Deep in the posterior throat area to catch pooling water
options.c: Close to the tooth with the bevel facing the cheek or tongue
options.d: Close to the tooth being treated, bevel facing the tooth

distractorExplanations.a: Placing the tip away from the working tooth lets spray and debris escape; it belongs at the tooth being treated.
distractorExplanations.b: Placing the tip near the soft palate or throat triggers the gag reflex; the saliva ejector handles pooled fluid.
distractorExplanations.c: The bevel faces the tooth being prepared so spray is captured at its source, not the adjacent soft tissue.

danb-gc-readiness-check-chairside-004.explanation: Proper HVE placement captures spray/debris at the source while preserving access and soft-tissue protection. Keep the tip from blocking the operator's view.

options.a: Review medical history/allergies and confirm the planned procedure
options.b: Set out instruments for the next appointment after this patient
options.c: Take bitewing radiographs routinely before every restorative visit
options.d: Apply topical anesthetic before reviewing the patient's health history

distractorExplanations.b: Setting up for another patient does not prepare this one; the history update and procedure confirmation come first.
distractorExplanations.c: Radiographs are prescribed by the dentist based on need, not taken routinely before each restorative appointment.
distractorExplanations.d: Topical is applied after the medical history is reviewed, since allergies and medications may change the plan.

options.a: Explorer to shape occlusal anatomy before setting
options.b: Cleoid-discoid carver or similar amalgam carvers
options.c: Amalgam condenser with a serrated working end
options.d: Burnisher to remove excess amalgam from the margins

distractorExplanations.a: An explorer checks margins and detects caries; its fine tip is not designed to carve amalgam anatomy.
distractorExplanations.c: Condensers pack amalgam into the preparation; carving is done afterward with carvers such as the cleoid-discoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Burnishers smooth and adapt amalgam to the margins; they do not carve away excess or create anatomy.

options.a: Recapping the used needle with a two-handed technique
options.b: Choosing the anesthetic and dose for the dentist to inject
options.c: Preparing the syringe and monitoring the patient
options.d: Passing the syringe in front of the patient's eyes

distractorExplanations.a: Needles are recapped with a one-handed scoop or a recapping device, not two-handed, to prevent needlesticks.
distractorExplanations.b: Anesthetic choice and dose are the dentist's decisions; the assistant prepares the cartridge the dentist selects.
distractorExplanations.d: The syringe is passed below the patient's line of sight in the transfer zone to reduce anxiety.

danb-gc-readiness-check-chairside-007.explanation: Assistants prepare and support within state-allowed duties and watch for adverse reactions. Aspiration assistance follows office protocol.

options.a: Behind the patient's head, in the static zone
options.b: Across the patient's chest/near the chin area
options.c: Over the patient's face, where the operator's view is best
options.d: Beside the operator's hip, in the operator's zone

distractorExplanations.a: The static zone (about 12 to 2 o'clock for a right-handed operator) holds rarely used items; exchanges happen over the chest.
distractorExplanations.c: Passing over the face risks dropping instruments on the patient; transfers occur below the chin over the chest.
distractorExplanations.d: The operator's zone is where the dentist sits; the transfer zone is the area over the patient's chest.

danb-gc-readiness-check-chairside-008.explanation: The transfer zone is typically over the patient's chest near the chin for safe exchanges. This is where operator and assistant exchange instruments.

options.a: Separate the teeth slightly so the proximal contact can be checked with floss
options.b: Retract the gingiva so an impression captures the margin
options.c: Hold the rubber dam in place on the most distal tooth
options.d: Provide a temporary wall for proximal restorations during placement

distractorExplanations.a: Tooth separation is done with wedges or separators; the band itself replaces the missing proximal wall.
distractorExplanations.b: Gingival retraction uses retraction cord; matrix bands contain restorative material during placement.
distractorExplanations.c: The dam is anchored by a clamp on the most distal tooth; matrix bands form a wall for restorative material.

options.a: Stop, clear the airway/field, upright or turn the patient as needed
options.b: Place the patient in Trendelenburg to improve blood flow to the brain
options.c: Continue with HVE suction and ask the patient to breathe through the nose
options.d: Deliver abdominal thrusts immediately while the patient is supine

distractorExplanations.b: Trendelenburg is a syncope position; lowering the head of a coughing patient worsens aspiration risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Continuing treatment while the patient coughs risks aspiration; stop and protect the airway first.
distractorExplanations.d: A forceful cough means the airway is still moving air; abdominal thrusts are for complete obstruction.

danb-gc-readiness-check-chairside-010.explanation: Airway protection and patient positioning take priority when coughing/choking risk appears. Summon help if distress persists.

options.a: Holding a clear matrix strip for Class III composites
options.b: Holding a matrix band for Class II restorations
options.c: Securing a dental dam clamp on the anchor tooth
options.d: Holding a sectional matrix ring for posterior composites

distractorExplanations.a: Class III composites use a clear Mylar strip held by hand or wedges, not a Tofflemire retainer.
distractorExplanations.c: Dam clamps are placed with clamp forceps; the Tofflemire holds a circumferential matrix band.
distractorExplanations.d: Sectional matrices use a separating ring system, not the universal Tofflemire retainer.

options.a: Using the air-water syringe continuously to keep the site rinsed
options.b: Placing the saliva ejector instead of HVE during high-speed cutting
options.c: Retracting the cheek with fingers instead of a mirror or HVE tip
options.d: Using suction, retraction, and isolation appropriate to the procedure

distractorExplanations.a: Continuous water spray floods the field; the air-water syringe is used intermittently with suction.
distractorExplanations.b: A saliva ejector cannot capture handpiece spray and debris; HVE is used during high-speed preparation.
distractorExplanations.c: Finger retraction risks injury and contamination; the mirror and HVE tip retract soft tissue safely.

options.a: Multifluted finishing burs for smoothing restoration margins
options.b: Diamond polishing points used on the slow-speed contra-angle
options.c: Straight fissure or pear/round carbide burs
options.d: Large round burs on a slow-speed handpiece for enamel outline

distractorExplanations.a: Finishing burs with many fine flutes smooth restorations; they cut too slowly to establish outline form.
distractorExplanations.b: Polishing points produce luster on restorations; outline cutting uses carbide or diamond cutting burs at high speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Slow-speed large round burs remove soft decay near the pulp; enamel outline is cut at high speed.

danb-gc-readiness-check-chairside-013.explanation: Operative burs (pear, round, fissure) cut enamel/dentin for outline form. These burs are designed for cavity preparation.

options.a: Gently retract gingiva for margin access/impression quality
options.b: Seal the dentinal tubules before the final impression is taken
options.c: Hold the provisional crown in place while temporary cement sets
options.d: Absorb saliva so the tooth stays dry during bur preparation

distractorExplanations.b: Tubule sealing is done with desensitizers or liners; retraction cord displaces gingiva to expose margins.
distractorExplanations.c: Provisionals are held with finger or bite pressure; cord is placed before the impression, not under a temporary.
distractorExplanations.d: Cotton rolls and HVE control saliva; cord is packed in the sulcus to retract tissue and expose margins.

options.a: The arch being treated, using one clamp size for each arch
options.b: The patient's age, with winged clamps reserved for children's primary teeth
options.c: Tooth morphology and stability needs for the tooth being isolated
options.d: The shade of the rubber dam material being used

distractorExplanations.a: Clamps are chosen per tooth type and size (molar, premolar, anterior), not one per arch.
distractorExplanations.b: Wing choice depends on placement technique and tooth anatomy, not on the patient's age.
distractorExplanations.d: Dam color or thickness does not determine clamp size; tooth crown anatomy at the cervical line does.

options.a: Until the mix looks dry and crumbly for easier carving
options.b: At the highest speed for twice the labeled time
options.c: According to manufacturer time/speed settings
options.d: For the same time for all brands, about 30 seconds

distractorExplanations.a: A dry, crumbly mix is undertriturated; correct trituration gives a smooth, shiny, plastic mass.
distractorExplanations.b: Overtrituration makes the mix hot, sets it too fast and weakens it; follow the labeled time and speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Times vary by alloy and capsule spill size; a single universal time ignores manufacturer settings.

options.a: Ultraviolet curing lamps emitting around 365 nm wavelength
options.b: Heat from the curing unit's halogen bulb warming the resin
options.c: Moisture from the tooth reacting with the resin matrix
options.d: Visible-light curing units of appropriate wavelength/intensity

distractorExplanations.a: Modern composites use camphorquinone activated by visible blue light near 470 nm; UV units are obsolete.
distractorExplanations.b: Heat is a by-product; polymerization is triggered when the photoinitiator absorbs blue light.
distractorExplanations.c: Moisture contamination weakens composite; it does not initiate polymerization like water-setting cements.

options.a: A temporary cement or sedative base/temporary filling
options.b: A permanent luting cement for bonded all-ceramic crowns
options.c: A liner placed directly under composite restorations
options.d: A pit and fissure sealant for newly erupted molars

distractorExplanations.b: ZOE is weak and eugenol inhibits resin bonding, so it is not used to permanently cement bonded ceramics.
distractorExplanations.c: Eugenol inhibits resin polymerization, so ZOE is avoided under composite restorations.
distractorExplanations.d: Sealants are resin or glass ionomer materials; ZOE has no role in sealing pits and fissures.

danb-gc-readiness-check-materials-003.explanation: ZOE has sedative properties and is used for temporary cementation/restorations (with eugenol caveats for composites). It is used in selected cases.

options.a: Creates microscopic irregularities to improve micromechanical retention
options.b: Forms a direct chemical bond between enamel calcium and the resin monomers
options.c: Removes plaque and pellicle so the tooth looks whiter
options.d: Disinfects the preparation and seals open dentinal tubules

distractorExplanations.b: Etch-and-rinse bonding to enamel is micromechanical; chemical adhesion to calcium describes glass ionomer.
distractorExplanations.c: Pumice prophylaxis removes plaque; phosphoric acid etch dissolves enamel rods to create micropores.
distractorExplanations.d: Etch opens dentinal tubules rather than sealing them, and disinfection is not its purpose in bonding.

options.a: After 24 hours, once the alginate has fully set
options.b: After soaking in water for 30 minutes to rehydrate
options.c: Within 7 days if sealed in a plastic bag
options.d: Promptly, ideally soon after removal

distractorExplanations.a: Alginate loses water (syneresis) and distorts within minutes; it is poured promptly, not a day later.
distractorExplanations.b: Soaking causes imbibition and swelling; a damp towel is used for a short delay, without submerging.
distractorExplanations.c: A multi-day pour window applies to elastomers such as PVS, not alginate, which distorts quickly.

danb-gc-readiness-check-materials-005.explanation: Alginate is dimensionally unstable with syneresis/imbibition; pour soon and store properly if delayed briefly. Keep it moist if a brief delay is unavoidable.

options.a: Needing more water per powder, which makes it stronger
options.b: Having lower water/powder ratio needs and greater strength
options.c: Setting faster and harder because it contains resin
options.d: Being softer, so it is preferred for working dies

distractorExplanations.a: Stone needs less water than plaster; extra water weakens any gypsum product.
distractorExplanations.c: Stone is calcium sulfate hemihydrate like plaster; its denser particles, not resin, make it stronger.
distractorExplanations.d: Working dies use high-strength stone (Type IV/V); plaster is the softer gypsum used for mounting and study models.

danb-gc-readiness-check-materials-006.explanation: Stone particles require less water and produce stronger casts than plaster. Type III stone is the usual comparison with plaster.

options.a: Chemical adhesion to tooth structure and fluoride release
options.b: Higher wear resistance than amalgam on occlusal surfaces
options.c: Insensitivity to moisture during the initial set
options.d: Superior esthetics compared with composite resin

distractorExplanations.b: Glass ionomers wear faster than amalgam and composite, which limits them in stress-bearing areas.
distractorExplanations.c: Early GIC is sensitive to moisture contamination and drying; it is protected with varnish or resin.
distractorExplanations.d: Composite is more esthetic; GIC is more opaque and is chosen for fluoride release and adhesion.

options.a: Record the margins of a crown preparation
options.b: Take a preliminary impression for study models
options.c: Fabricate a provisional crown chairside
options.d: Record occlusal relationship between arches

distractorExplanations.a: Margin detail is captured with a final impression material, not with a bite registration.
distractorExplanations.b: Study models come from alginate preliminary impressions; bite registration records how the arches meet.
distractorExplanations.c: Provisionals use bis-acryl or acrylic resin; bite registration material records occlusion.

options.a: Base and catalyst mixed to a uniform color per instructions
options.b: Light curing in increments after seating the tray
options.c: A spatulated mix with water to a creamy consistency
options.d: An adhesive-free tray so the material releases cleanly

distractorExplanations.b: Polysulfide sets by chemical reaction after mixing; light curing applies to composites and some tray resins.
distractorExplanations.c: Water mixing applies to alginate and gypsum; polysulfide is a two-paste base/catalyst system.
distractorExplanations.d: Elastomers such as polysulfide need tray adhesive so the material does not pull away and distort.

options.a: Bond composite resin to dentin in shallow preparations
options.b: Stimulate reparative dentin / protect pulp in deep preparations
options.c: Insulate the pulp from heat under metal restorations as a thick base
options.d: Release fluoride and bond chemically to tooth structure

distractorExplanations.a: Bonding is done with adhesive systems; calcium hydroxide has no bond strength and dissolves over time.
distractorExplanations.c: Thick insulating bases are typically ZOE, zinc phosphate or GIC; Ca(OH)2 is applied as a thin liner.
distractorExplanations.d: Fluoride release and chemical bonding describe glass ionomer liners, not calcium hydroxide.

danb-gc-readiness-check-materials-010.explanation: Ca(OH)2 liners are used for pulp protection/indirect-direct pulp capping strategies as indicated. It is placed when indicated.

options.a: Be cemented with permanent cement to prevent dislodgement
options.b: Be left slightly high so the patient bites them into place
options.c: Protect the preparation and be cemented temporarily
options.d: Have margins short of the finish line to protect the gingiva

distractorExplanations.a: Provisionals use temporary cement so the dentist can remove them at the final delivery visit.
distractorExplanations.b: High occlusion causes soreness and pressure on the tooth; provisionals are adjusted to normal occlusion.
distractorExplanations.d: Short margins leave dentin exposed and allow sensitivity; provisional margins should match the preparation.

danb-gc-readiness-check-materials-011.explanation: Provisionals protect pulp/periodontium, maintain space and function until final delivery. They should also maintain contacts and occlusion.

options.a: Offer excellent dimensional stability and detail reproduction
options.b: Must be poured within 15 minutes to avoid distortion
options.c: Set by light curing, allowing unlimited working time
options.d: Release ethyl alcohol during setting, which keeps them flexible

distractorExplanations.b: That is the alginate rule; PVS remains stable for days and can be poured later per the manufacturer.
distractorExplanations.c: PVS is an addition-reaction silicone that sets chemically after mixing; its working time is limited.
distractorExplanations.d: Ethyl alcohol by-product release describes condensation silicones, which shrink over time; PVS has none.

options.a: Glass ionomer setting when it is used as a base under amalgam
options.b: Zinc phosphate cement setting reaction
options.c: Composite resin polymerization/bonding if contaminated
options.d: Amalgam condensation over a ZOE temporary base or liner

distractorExplanations.a: Glass ionomer sets by an acid-base reaction unaffected by eugenol; eugenol mainly inhibits resin systems.
distractorExplanations.b: Zinc phosphate sets by an acid-base reaction; eugenol interference is a resin polymerization problem.
distractorExplanations.d: Amalgam is commonly placed over ZOE-type bases without setting problems; eugenol inhibits resin polymerization.

options.a: Leave a rough surface that will smooth itself out during normal chewing
options.b: Discolor adjacent composite restorations from amalgam dust
options.c: Damage the restoration because final set strength develops over time
options.d: Weaken bonding because amalgam bonds chemically to enamel

distractorExplanations.a: Early polishing does not leave roughness that self-corrects; it risks fracturing margins of incompletely set amalgam.
distractorExplanations.b: Dust discoloring nearby restorations is not the concern; amalgam reaches full strength after about 24 hours.
distractorExplanations.d: Conventional amalgam is retained mechanically, not bonded chemically; the concern is incomplete set strength.

options.a: Brushing right after every acidic drink or snack to remove the acid from enamel
options.b: Daily fluoride toothpaste use, plaque control, and limiting frequent sugar exposures
options.c: Using a whitening toothpaste twice daily instead of a regular fluoride-containing toothpaste
options.d: Rinsing with an alcohol-based mouthwash after meals in place of daily flossing

distractorExplanations.a: Brushing right after acidic intake can abrade softened enamel; fluoride, plaque control and diet are the core strategy.
distractorExplanations.c: Whitening pastes target stains; fluoride toothpaste is what strengthens enamel against caries.
distractorExplanations.d: Mouthwash does not remove interproximal plaque; floss or interdental cleaners are still needed.

options.a: Remove calculus deposits below the gumline between teeth
options.b: Clean the occlusal pits and fissures of posterior teeth
options.c: Deliver fluoride to the proximal enamel of the teeth
options.d: Clean interproximal surfaces where brushes may not reach

distractorExplanations.a: Calculus is hardened and must be removed by professional scaling; floss disrupts soft plaque biofilm.
distractorExplanations.b: Floss cannot reach pits and fissures; it cleans proximal surfaces, while sealants and brushing protect occlusals.
distractorExplanations.c: Floss is a mechanical plaque-removal aid; fluoride comes from toothpaste, rinses and varnish.

options.a: Finish the step quickly, then give oxygen
options.b: Be placed supine with legs raised and given glucose
options.c: Stop treatment, follow emergency protocol
options.d: Take aspirin and continue after the pain eases

distractorExplanations.a: Chest pain requires stopping treatment immediately; finishing the procedure delays emergency care.
distractorExplanations.b: Glucose treats hypoglycemia and legs-raised positioning treats syncope; angina calls for NTG and oxygen, usually seated upright.
distractorExplanations.d: Elective care stops with chest pain; aspirin may be part of a suspected-MI protocol, but resuming treatment is unsafe.

danb-gc-readiness-check-patient-care-003.explanation: Chest pain is a medical emergency pathway: stop dentistry and activate emergency response per training. This includes nitroglycerin if prescribed, oxygen, and EMS as indicated.

options.a: Intraoral examination of the tongue and floor of the mouth alone
options.b: Visual inspection with biopsy of any lesion by the dental assistant
options.c: Extraoral and intraoral soft-tissue examination and referral
options.d: Rechecking red or white lesions at the next 12-month recall visit

distractorExplanations.a: Screening covers the head and neck extraorally plus every intraoral site, not just the tongue and floor of mouth.
distractorExplanations.b: Assistants may help with screening, but biopsy is performed by the dentist or a specialist after referral.
distractorExplanations.d: Suspicious red or white lesions are re-evaluated in about 2 weeks or referred, not watched for a year.

danb-gc-readiness-check-patient-care-004.explanation: Systematic soft-tissue exam and timely referral are standard prevention roles. Suspicious lesions are referred promptly.

options.a: Use powder-free latex gloves to reduce airborne allergens
options.b: Pre-medicate with an antihistamine and use latex gloves
options.c: Schedule as the last patient of the day to limit exposure
options.d: Use non-latex gloves and avoid latex products in the operatory

distractorExplanations.a: Powder-free latex lowers airborne protein but still contains latex; allergic patients need non-latex products.
distractorExplanations.b: Premedication does not make latex exposure safe; the allergen must be eliminated from the operatory.
distractorExplanations.c: Latex-allergic patients are scheduled first in the day, when airborne latex particles are lowest.

options.a: Seal pits and fissures on newly erupted molars
options.b: Etch enamel before orthodontic bracket bonding
options.c: Reduce caries risk on enamel surfaces per protocol
options.d: Remove extrinsic stains after a prophylaxis

distractorExplanations.a: Sealing pits and fissures is the job of sealants; varnish releases fluoride but does not form a lasting seal.
distractorExplanations.b: Etching uses phosphoric acid; fluoride varnish is applied for caries prevention, not to prepare enamel for bonding.
distractorExplanations.d: Stains are removed with prophy paste or polishing; varnish leaves a temporary film that delivers fluoride.

options.a: Proximal surfaces of premolars with early enamel lesions
options.b: Smooth facial surfaces of anterior teeth after orthodontic bracket removal
options.c: Caries-susceptible pits and fissures of posterior teeth when indicated
options.d: Root surfaces exposed by gingival recession in older adults

distractorExplanations.a: Sealants are placed on occlusal pits and fissures; proximal lesions are managed with fluoride or restoration.
distractorExplanations.b: Smooth surfaces lack deep fissures for retention; white-spot lesions there are treated with fluoride.
distractorExplanations.d: Root caries risk is managed with fluoride varnish or high-fluoride paste; sealants target occlusal fissures.

options.a: Stop warfarin 5 days before the extraction on the dentist's order
options.b: Switch to aspirin the week before surgery to reduce bleeding
options.c: Have medical consultation regarding bleeding risk and INR management
options.d: Have bleeding time tested by the dental office on the morning of surgery

distractorExplanations.a: Stopping warfarin raises thrombosis risk; any change is made by the prescribing physician, and many extractions proceed with INR in range.
distractorExplanations.b: Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug that also increases bleeding; it does not replace warfarin management.
distractorExplanations.d: Warfarin is monitored with the INR (PT), not bleeding time; the INR is typically checked within 24 hours of surgery.

danb-gc-readiness-check-patient-care-008.explanation: Anticoagulation management requires coordination; do not unilaterally stop meds. Medical input is sought as indicated.

options.a: Bristles at 90 degrees to the tooth with firm horizontal strokes
options.b: A medium-bristle brush with firm pressure to remove plaque faster
options.c: Angled bristles aimed toward the occlusal surface, away from the gumline
options.d: Gentle angled bristles at the gingival margin covering all surfaces

distractorExplanations.a: Horizontal scrubbing with firm pressure causes abrasion and recession; bristles are angled about 45° into the sulcus.
distractorExplanations.b: Soft brushes with gentle pressure are recommended; firm pressure and stiffer bristles injure the gingiva.
distractorExplanations.c: In the Bass method bristles point apically into the sulcus at about 45°, not toward the occlusal surface.

danb-gc-readiness-check-patient-care-009.explanation: Effective plaque removal with minimal trauma uses proper angulation and gentle pressure. The Bass technique is the classic example.

options.a: Dry mouth raises oral pH, which favors acid-producing bacteria
options.b: Medications that cause dry mouth directly dissolve enamel
options.c: Less saliva means more calculus forms on enamel
options.d: Saliva normally buffers acids and aids remineralization

distractorExplanations.a: Saliva loss lowers buffering so pH stays acidic longer; a lower pH, not a raised pH, favors caries.
distractorExplanations.b: Xerogenic drugs reduce saliva flow; they do not dissolve enamel themselves.
distractorExplanations.c: Calculus is plaque mineralized from saliva; xerostomia's caries effect comes from lost buffering and clearance.

options.a: Explaining, demonstrating on a model/finger, then performing the step
options.b: Showing the instrument first, then explaining, then performing the step
options.c: Telling the child what will happen, then doing it without demonstration
options.d: Praising the child after the step to reinforce good behavior

distractorExplanations.b: The order is tell, then show, then do; explanation in child-friendly words comes before the demonstration.
distractorExplanations.c: Skipping the show step removes the demonstration that reduces fear; the three steps are used in order.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes positive reinforcement, a separate behavior guidance technique, not tell-show-do.

options.a: An AED and blood pressure cuff, with medications kept by EMS
options.b: Oxygen and emergency medications per ADA/office protocol
options.c: Nitroglycerin and morphine for chest pain, without oxygen
options.d: Local anesthetic cartridges and sedatives for anxious patients

distractorExplanations.a: An AED is recommended, but offices must stock basic drugs such as epinephrine and nitroglycerin; EMS may be minutes away.
distractorExplanations.c: Morphine is not a basic kit drug for dental offices, and oxygen is a core item in every emergency kit.
distractorExplanations.d: Anesthetics and sedatives are treatment drugs, not emergency drugs; the kit holds oxygen, epinephrine and similar.

danb-gc-readiness-check-patient-care-012.explanation: Offices maintain oxygen and emergency drugs matched to anticipated emergencies and training. Examples include epinephrine and an antihistamine.

options.a: Postponing all dental radiographs until after delivery
options.b: Elective care timing discussion and avoiding unnecessary radiographs
options.c: Treating elective care in the first trimester before the fetus grows
options.d: Delaying treatment of dental infections until after the birth

distractorExplanations.a: Necessary radiographs may be taken during pregnancy with ALARA and shielding; they are not banned outright.
distractorExplanations.c: The second trimester is the preferred time for elective care; the first trimester is the period of organogenesis.
distractorExplanations.d: Untreated infection is a greater risk to mother and fetus; urgent care proceeds during pregnancy.

danb-gc-readiness-check-patient-care-013.explanation: Coordinate timing, use ALARA with shielding, and treat infection to protect mother/fetus. Urgent care proceeds as needed with shielding.

options.a: Dental biofilm (plaque) and host response
options.b: Calculus deposits that irritate the gingiva
options.c: Traumatic occlusion from bruxism
options.d: Vitamin C deficiency in the diet

distractorExplanations.b: Calculus is a plaque-retentive factor, but living biofilm is the primary cause of periodontal inflammation.
distractorExplanations.c: Occlusal trauma can modify bone loss but does not initiate gingival inflammation; plaque biofilm does.
distractorExplanations.d: Nutritional deficiency can worsen tissue response, but bacterial biofilm is the primary etiology.

options.a: Rinsing vigorously with warm salt water every hour on the day of surgery
options.b: Applying heat packs to the face for the first 24 hours
options.c: Biting on gauze, avoiding straws/smoking, and soft diet as instructed
options.d: Using a straw for liquids so food avoids the extraction site

distractorExplanations.a: Rinsing is delayed until about 24 hours after extraction to avoid dislodging the clot.
distractorExplanations.b: Cold packs are used in the first 24 hours to limit swelling; moist heat may be used later if advised.
distractorExplanations.d: Straw suction can dislodge the clot and cause dry socket; drinking from a cup is advised.

options.a: Kept confidential and secured per HIPAA and office policy
options.b: Released to the patient's employer on request for insurance
options.c: Kept for one year after the last visit, then shredded
options.d: Shared freely among staff, since all employees are covered

distractorExplanations.b: Employers are not entitled to PHI without the patient's written authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Retention periods are set by state law and are typically several years, not one year after the last visit.
distractorExplanations.d: HIPAA's minimum necessary standard limits access to what each role needs, even within the office.

options.a: Risks, benefits, alternatives, and patient agreement
options.b: The fee estimate and the insurance coverage breakdown
options.c: The procedure name and the patient's signature
options.d: Benefits and alternatives, with risks discussed if asked

distractorExplanations.b: Financial consent is separate; informed consent covers the risks, benefits and alternatives of treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: A name and signature without a discussion of risks, benefits and alternatives is not informed consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Material risks must be disclosed proactively; consent cannot leave out risks unless the patient asks.

options.a: Increase daily production by double-booking short visits
options.b: Reduce the number of broken appointments and no-shows
options.c: Support quality care and reduce stress/errors
options.d: Allow the assistant to perform procedures unsupervised

distractorExplanations.a: Double-booking increases rushing and errors; adequate time for complex procedures protects quality.
distractorExplanations.b: Confirmation calls and reminders reduce no-shows; scheduling enough procedure time is about quality and safety.
distractorExplanations.d: Scheduling does not change supervision rules; delegated duties follow state dental practice law.

options.a: Posting SDS only for chemicals with a skull symbol
options.b: Labeling secondary containers just when they are stored overnight
options.c: Training employees once at hire with no updates for new chemicals
options.d: Maintaining SDS access and labeling for hazardous chemicals

distractorExplanations.a: SDS must be available for every hazardous chemical in the office, not just those with the acute-toxicity pictogram.
distractorExplanations.b: Secondary containers need labels whenever chemicals are transferred, unless used immediately by the person who filled them.
distractorExplanations.c: HazCom training is required at hire and whenever a new hazardous chemical is introduced.

options.a: Mechanical and chemical monitoring, with spore tests run once a month per unit
options.b: Mechanical, chemical, and biological (spore) monitoring per CDC guidance
options.c: Chemical indicators on every pouch in place of spore testing
options.d: Daily Bowie-Dick tests for all tabletop gravity sterilizers

distractorExplanations.a: CDC recommends spore testing at least weekly for each sterilizer, not monthly.
distractorExplanations.c: Chemical indicators show process conditions but cannot replace biological spore tests that confirm kill.
distractorExplanations.d: Bowie-Dick tests are for prevacuum (dynamic air removal) sterilizers; gravity tabletop units are monitored with spore tests.

options.a: Explain risks/benefits/limitations and document refusal
options.b: Have the patient sign a waiver releasing the office from liability
options.c: Proceed with treatment using last year's radiographs only
options.d: Refer the patient to another office without documenting it

distractorExplanations.b: Patients cannot consent to negligent care; a liability waiver does not replace informed refusal documentation.
distractorExplanations.c: Outdated images may not show current disease; the dentist decides whether care can proceed safely.
distractorExplanations.d: Refusal must be documented in the chart; a referral without documentation leaves no record of informed refusal.

danb-gc-readiness-check-office-007.explanation: Respect autonomy with informed refusal documentation; some care may be deferred if unsafe without imaging. Then determine if care can proceed safely.

options.a: Storing full and empty cylinders together lying on the floor
options.b: Securing cylinders and checking connections for leaks
options.c: Testing for leaks by listening for hissing at the regulator
options.d: Storing nitrous oxide cylinders next to the autoclave for warmth

distractorExplanations.a: Cylinders are stored upright and secured, with full and empty tanks separated and labeled.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaks are checked with soapy solution or a detector; listening misses small leaks that expose staff to N2O.
distractorExplanations.d: Cylinders are kept away from heat sources; heat raises internal pressure and creates a rupture hazard.

danb-gc-readiness-check-office-008.explanation: Compressed gas safety and scavenging protect patients and staff. Follow scavenger system protocols.

options.a: Use the instruments if the spore test from last week passed
options.b: Wipe the instruments with disinfectant and use them on the patient
options.c: Run a spore test and use the load while waiting for results
options.d: Not use the load; reprocess and investigate per protocol

distractorExplanations.a: A prior spore test does not clear a current load whose indicator shows conditions were not met.
distractorExplanations.b: Disinfection is not sterilization; critical instruments from a failed load must be reprocessed.
distractorExplanations.c: A failed chemical indicator means the load is not used; it is not released while spore results are pending.

options.a: Contact patients about outstanding account balances
options.b: Schedule preventive visits and periodontal maintenance
options.c: Confirm the next day's appointments by phone
options.d: Track lab cases sent out for crowns and dentures

distractorExplanations.a: Collections are an accounts receivable task; recall systems schedule preventive and maintenance visits.
distractorExplanations.c: Appointment confirmation is a separate daily task; recall tracks when patients are due for preventive care.
distractorExplanations.d: Lab case tracking is a separate system; recall brings patients back for hygiene and periodontal maintenance.

options.a: Washing gloved hands between patients and reusing the same gloves
options.b: Hand hygiene, PPE changes, surface barriers, and instrument sterilization
options.c: Disinfecting barrier-covered surfaces first and then removing the barriers
options.d: Cold-sterilizing handpieces in disinfectant between patients

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves are single-use; washing them damages the material, and they are changed between patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Barriers are removed and replaced between patients; the surface is disinfected after removal if the barrier failed.
distractorExplanations.d: Handpieces are heat sterilized between patients; immersion in disinfectant is not acceptable for them.

danb-gc-readiness-check-office-013.explanation: Standard infection-control chains interrupt pathogen transmission. These steps are repeated between patients.

options.a: Workforce members with PHI access need training appropriate to their roles
options.b: Training is required once at hire, with no further updates needed later on
options.c: Front-desk staff need training, but clinical assistants do not
options.d: Training applies to electronic records, not to paper charts

distractorExplanations.b: Training is also required when policies change materially; one-time training ignores policy updates.
distractorExplanations.c: Every workforce member who handles PHI, including clinical staff, must be trained.
distractorExplanations.d: HIPAA privacy rules cover PHI in every form, including paper and spoken information.

options.a: Responding to the patient's online review with visit details
options.b: Listening, documenting, and following office resolution policy
options.c: Referring the patient to the state dental board so the board can resolve it
options.d: Offering a fee refund before hearing the full complaint

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosing visit details in a public review response violates HIPAA; complaints are handled privately.
distractorExplanations.c: Staff conduct complaints are resolved in-office first; the dental board handles licensure and practice issues.
distractorExplanations.d: Refunds before listening skip documentation and investigation; the complaint is heard and recorded first.

danb-gc-readiness-check-office-015.explanation: Professional complaint handling protects relationships and risk management. Escalate per policy and stay professional.
